My wife tried to phone our neighbor because she was feeling unsafe and called her bother who could speak Spanish with installer. Nothing helped. He was getting very amped up. She told him there was nothing wrong with our old air gap. He refused to return the old air gap to my wife. We finally told him to install new one just so we could get this over and him out of the situation where he was aggressive to my wife. The new air gap he installed isn't even installed upright correctly and has a slight lean. My wife refused to pay until we got an invoice. I spoke with Transmotion a couple times after that (they called that same day trying to get payment). When I explained what happened the rep said someone from Transmotion would contact me to resolve. Never happened, although they did try to contact me several times to get me to pay. Costco was awesome in helping us resolve the situation, but I would highly recommend you avoid Transmotion installation! We've never had an installation experience like this through Costco before. It does make me think twice about buying future appliances from Costco if they come with installation.

Sentence (English): Bought as a replacement for an ailing dishwasher that was almost 23 years old so will be a while before we can comment on longevity.
Comments (English): [ Quiet and efficient ] || ---------------- || Bought as a replacement for an ailing dishwasher that was almost 23 years old so will be a while before we can comment on longevity. However it seems improvements have been made over the decades and this item is certainly significantly quieter. Looking at energy useage it is much lower energy use and doesn't spike the current draw from our battery system. Space inside the unit is excellent with lots of useable options for different cooking utensils and just generally a lot of space. The top drawer for cutlery in particular is excellent and heeps the possibly sharper items safely out of the way. It's easy to setup and although I have the app and wifi connection, I generally wonder why. Not relly sure this adds anything of practical use. Cleaning of items has generally been pretty good with a slight learning experience required in how to stack to avoid missing bits. The eco cycle seems to work fine for pretty much all occasions, unless there are some seriously baked and dried on food which can still leave traces. The time of the eco cycle is amazingly long at approaching 5 hours although to be fair just over an hour of this is the final drying and cooldown with the door open at the end. The fact that the door springs open to complete drying was a bit of a surprise, but works fine and we do have a well ventilated kitchen so not an issue.

Sentence (English): We replaced an LG dishwasher that just wasn't cleaning dishes well.
Comments (English): [ BOSCH 800 Series Dishwasher ] || ---------------- || We replaced an LG dishwasher that just wasn't cleaning dishes well. This BOSCH dishwasher has done a great job at cleaning the dishes. It claims you don't need to pre-rinse food, just scrap off the remains, that is how you're supposed to save X number of gallons of water. So far, it's cleaning dishes that have sat in the dishwasher a couple of days. The third rack on the top is great for smaller things to be set up there, like my travel coffee cup lids, spatulas, long handled serving spoons, etc. I wasn't sure how clean it will get things without a direct water source under the shelf, but so far everything looks and feels clean. With that said, I do have one big complaint. You have to spend too much time trying to figure out how to put certain items in. The bottom rack is awful for trying to put more than a couple of different shaped items in it due to the angle and spacing of the prongs to support the items. The dishes are a breeze, but everything else it's a game of Tetris. We've been using it for a month and I still haven't had an "ah-ha" moment to easily figure it out. Also, the silverware cubby openings are slightly too small for our heavy duty silverware ends to easily slide in. The dinner forks are the biggest challenge at getting them out. I am thinking I need to make some cuts in the plastic spacers to eliminate the wrestling. I do not want to resort to using the uppermost third rack for them. If I could rate on how dishwasher performs only, it would be 5 stars. The layout of the shelves and silverware would only get a 3.

Sentence (English): Yes, we bought our first Bosch dishwasher in 1999.
Comments (English): [ A great replacement for our 1999 vintage! ] || ---------------- || Yes, we bought our first Bosch dishwasher in 1999. We loved it for its efficiency, but also how, compared to other makes, it was very quiet. Guests could not believe it was running. About a couple of years ago it developed an intermittent problem which was diagnosed as an issue with the “mother board”. We lived with it rather than replace the expensive part, but at nearly 25 years of age we decided to replace it with a new appliance. We are certainly glad we did as the new model now makes the older one seem noisy, and it really needs that light that lets you no it is running. We have been amazed how many adjustments you can make to the racks and fittings inside the dishwasher – we have yet to use it with the middle rack set at an angle! The ability to clean heavily soiled plates and dishes is excellent. With the various drying options, one can optimize for a particular load, but we have found one that works perfectly with any load, including glassware. We heartily recommend this dishwater, and just hope it is reliable as our earlier dishwasher was.

Comments (English): [ Functional, but with interface flaws ] || ---------------- || We got this to replace a much older Bosch dishwasher which had always worked well, but that lacked a much desired feature- a delayed start setting. It came down to this or the other premium German dishwasher, and we chose the Bosch mostly on the basis good previous experience. Overall, it's a nice upgrade, with- in our view- one big flaw. It turns out that the delayed start function cannot be accessed on the dishwasher controls directly, but REQUIRES that you use an app on your phone to set a delay time. That's a completely unnecessary level of complexity- you have to set the dishwasher to start, then go to the app to set the time. Other dishwashers we have used just let you set a delay- 1,2, 3 hours, etc. On the brighter side, it works extremely well, and it is so quiet that the delayed start function is less important than it was with our previous unit. The trays are well configured to hold what we put in, and things do come out mostly very dry without excess heat. So overall we are very pleased, but as user interface designers ourselves this requirement to go to another device in order to access a pretty basic function just seems wrong.

Sentence (English): We replaced an LG dishwasher that just wasn't cleaning dishes well.
Comments (English): [ BOSCH 800 Series Dishwasher ] || ---------------- || We replaced an LG dishwasher that just wasn't cleaning dishes well. This BOSCH dishwasher has done a great job at cleaning the dishes. It claims you don't need to pre-rinse food, just scrap off the remains, that is how you're supposed to save X number of gallons of water. So far, it's cleaning dishes that have sat in the dishwasher a couple of days. The third rack on the top is great for smaller things to be set up there, like my travel coffee cup lids, spatulas, long handled serving spoons, etc. I wasn't sure how clean it will get things without a direct water source under the shelf, but so far everything looks and feels clean.With that said, I do have one big complaint. You have to spend too much time trying to figure out how to put certain items in. The bottom rack is awful for trying to put more than a couple of different shaped items in it due to the angle and spacing of the prongs to support the items. The dishes are a breeze, but everything else it's a game of Tetris. We've been using it for a month and I still haven't had an "ah-ha" moment to easily figure it out. Also, the silverware cubby openings are slightly too small for our heavy duty silverware ends to easily slide in. The dinner forks are the biggest challenge at getting them out. I am thinking I need to make some cuts in the plastic spacers to eliminate the wrestling. I do not want to resort to using the uppermost third rack for them.If I could rate on how dishwasher performs only, it would be 5 stars. The layout of the shelves and silverware would only get a 3.

Sentence (English): We have had this dishwasher for a couple months now.
Comments (English): [ Great dishwasher but needs a few improvements ] || ---------------- || We have had this dishwasher for a couple months now. It really does a great job cleaning my dishes. After every wash, I'm always amazed on how clean and shiny they are. I've always washed my pots and pans by hand but thought I would try and see if this dishwasher really did what it claimed. and it did! You can also wash plastic containers without having to worry about melting. My pots and pans look like new after I run them through the dishwasher. Cleaning up after dinner is so much quicker now that I don't have to wash a few things by hand. We usually run the dishwasher at night so by morning everything does seem to be dry. The silverware basket is a bit small but now that I'm used to using the top tray, I don't really use it much, which gives you a little more room on the bottom tray. This dishwasher does has a smaller cavity than my previous one.A few things that I thought should be improved in the manufacturing of this product are as follows: The design of the pull-out handle should be more rounded as it would be more comfortable on the hand and/ or a little bit more inset so that it will not scratch the door. The bottom drawer handle seems to touch the door, which leaves a permanent scratch line. This dishwasher seems to be "welded" on the bottom and outer sides. Maybe there should be better quality control to make sure ther is no sharp edges at the seams. There should be an improvement made in the assembly of the cavity as there was some roughness along the welded edges with little tiny pieces of metal, which caused a cut on my finger. I do love how this dishwasher cleans your dishes etc. but it could use some manufacturing redesign on the inside.

So far we aren't really impressed. The biggest problem is that the trays are so specialized that you end up without a lot of flexibility. For example, the top rack is designed for glasses, but the center area of the top rack doesn't work well for short glasses because of the way the tilt is designed. The bottom rack doesn't let you put in two rows of large dishes, not because there isn't enough room, but because the wire grid is spaced such that the dishes roll into each other. Also I find that even the slightest brush of my hand across the control surface activates a bunch of controls. This means that if I reach down and close the door with my open palm, it thinks I pushed a lot of buttons. Frankly we miss our old dishwasher. On a positive note, it does seem to dry well with the newly included fan.

Sentence (English): This dishwasher looks great and is simple yet sophisticated enough for all household needs.
Comments (English): [ Great when it works . Disappointed after 1 year ] || ---------------- || This dishwasher looks great and is simple yet sophisticated enough for all household needs. Installation was easy and things worked beautifully until we hit the one year mark. Using the tech sheet we were able to troubleshoot things and fix it . for a little while. Installation was easy and things worked beautifully until we hit the one year mark. Using the tech sheet we were able to troubleshoot things and fix it . for a little while. We would go a week or so before the drying wouldn't happen and then it was every few days and now we cannot make it through a single wash. Unfortunately, a breaker seems to trip early in the wash cycle now so the water is not even heating for the wash. Our dishes come back unsanitized, wet, and smelly. The bottom area that lets all the water out will not let the water out when it is cold (most of the water is released through evaporation) so it pools up at the bottom and smells awful. Very disappointing to have such trouble within such a short amount of time with only moderate use on RO system water with mostly clean dishes being washed since we use a septic system and do not run any dishes with food through our dishwasher. I should also mention that we live in a very rural area without in person appliance support so a lot of the troubleshooting has to be us. We ordered and replaced many parts but the troubling thing is the inconsistency in failure. Now the system is officially consistently failing so that leaves us with replacing the main computer or the dishwasher. Overall though, we specifically sought an American made product to include into our kitchen remodel and were thrilled at the beginning. Since about the 1 year mark we have unfortunately been incredibly disappointed in this specific product. To make matters worse, the dishwasher trim is also starting to come off. Wishing you all the best on your GE appliance search. I am sure there are good ones out there but I would definitely pass this dishwasher by.

Instructions on the various panel options and combinations are lacking, but are fairly intuitive so not a big deal. The unit is fairly quiet, and has been doing a good job on the first few runs. I'm not convinced the very top rack is particularly useful, as there are only a few inches of clearance in there. My first thought was tupperware lids, but they retain a pool of water after the cycle since they are laying flat. Sentence (English): We have had this dishwasher for a couple months now.
Comments (English): [ Great dishwasher but needs a few improvements ] || ---------------- || We have had this dishwasher for a couple months now. It really does a great job cleaning my dishes. After every wash, I'm always amazed on how clean and shiny they are. I've always washed my pots and pans by hand but thought I would try and see if this dishwasher really did what it claimed. and it did! You can also wash plastic containers without having to worry about melting. My pots and pans look like new after I run them through the dishwasher. Cleaning up after dinner is so much quicker now that I don't have to wash a few things by hand. We usually run the dishwasher at night so by morning everything does seem to be dry. The silverware basket is a bit small but now that I'm used to using the top tray, I don't really use it much, which gives you a little more room on the bottom tray. This dishwasher does has a smaller cavity than my previous one. A few things that I thought should be improved in the manufacturing of this product are as follows: The design of the pull-out handle should be more rounded as it would be more comfortable on the hand and/ or a little bit more inset so that it will not scratch the door. The bottom drawer handle seems to touch the door, which leaves a permanent scratch line. This dishwasher seems to be "welded" on the bottom and outer sides. Maybe there should be better quality control to make sure ther is no sharp edges at the seams. There should be an improvement made in the assembly of the cavity as there was some roughness along the welded edges with little tiny pieces of metal, which caused a cut on my finger. I do love how this dishwasher cleans your dishes etc. but it could use some manufacturing redesign on the inside.

Sentence (English): Overall, I believe that we will be happy with our Bosch 300 series dishwasher.
Comments (English): [ Fine machine, but some issues ] || ---------------- || Overall, I believe that we will be happy with our Bosch 300 series dishwasher. It will take some adjusting to get used to the rack setup. We do like the shallow, uppermost rack. The middle rack for glasses does not accommodate wider glasses well. The side parts of the rack are quite narrow, and in the middle it is too loose to support the cups. The slots for plates are so tightly put together that we have to just use every other slot. We did not receive a paper manual, since the company is being "green". That is fine, but we found it challenging to get it. The Bosch website indicated that the Model number would show on the top lip of the door. It was not there. Eventually, we found out if was on the right side of the door (very hard to reach since it was tightly in the corner (see photo). I could only find it by sliding my iPhone in a narrow crack and shooting random photos until I captured the image. At that point the person at Bosch guided us through being able to download the manual. "Finish" detergent and drying agent were recommended and samples were given. Dishes came out nice and clean, but were heavily perfumed, to the degree that it affected the taste of food or drink used with the clean dishes/glasses. Who needs perfumed dishes!

Sentence (English): We upgraded to this dishwasher recently, and I LOVE it!
Comments (English): [ So glad we upgraded!  ] || ---------------- || We upgraded to this dishwasher recently, and I LOVE it! Our last one was only 2.5 years old, a Whirlpool from Costco in the $500-600 range. It worked ok, but left brown residue (perhaps from our hard water), and over time stopped cleaning dishes very well. I'M SO GLAD WE UPGRADED! In many ways, it's just a solid, reliable dishwasher, perhaps not much different than others in the slightly cheaper range. But in other ways, it's a dream come true. Everyone is different, but for us: -Is the third rack worth it? YES! Every penny. -Is the extra efficient loading area helping? YES! Our big family now runs a load once a day instead of 3 every two days. -Are the racks noticeably better made? YES! They feel sturdy and roll well. -Is the water softener helping? I think so, though that's not why we bought it. I did buy it for the stainless steel tub, which handles hard water better and I've seen no build up! I also love the timer on the front so I always know how long till it's done. And we never rinse, just scrape off plates and put them right in!

Sentence (English): This thing does an incredible job of washing dishes.
Comments (English): [ Bosch 800 Dishwasher ] || ---------------- || This thing does an incredible job of washing dishes. Am of the old school where you had to wash the dishes BEFORE putting them in the dishwasher - but no more. Scrape, load, done. The machine does it all incredibly well. Not quite as quiet as the dishwasher it replaced, (39 db vs 42 db) but still comfortably within the tolerable range. Rack design is another story, though. The middle rack - ostensibly the one for glasses works well enough but seems a little awkward fitting glasses in. The holders for the stemware are not as universal fit as would (should? ) be expected. When folded down and out of the way, any glassware with an indented bottom sit too upright to allow collected water to just drain off. Glassware is sparkling clean but there's just a small puddle of water to be blotted up with a quick touch of a towel. Not quite as quiet as the dishwasher it replaced, (39 db vs 42 db) but still comfortably within the tolerable range. Rack design is another story, though. The middle rack - ostensibly the one for glasses works well enough but seems a little awkward fitting glasses in. The holders for the stemware are not as universal fit as would (should? ) be expected. When folded down and out of the way, any glassware with an indented bottom sit too upright to allow collected water to just drain off. Glassware is sparkling clean but there's just a small puddle of water to be blotted up with a quick touch of a towel. The tilt feature is a nice touch but not something I have used or expect to ever really need. Overall, it does a great job of washing dishes and am more than happy with it. The middle rack design is a let down more than a disappointment, but all things considered, am more than happy with this purchase

Sentence (English): This is our first Bosch, and we are excited to have a water softener in the dishwasher to combat our hard water!
Comments (English): [ DYI Installation and Control Panel Review ] || ---------------- || This is our first Bosch, and we are excited to have a water softener in the dishwasher to combat our hard water! The review was lowered a little do to installation and the control panel. We typically install our own appliances, but this one had challenges. The instruction manual was not understandable on a few issues, and we resorted to online videos foradditional help, such as whether to retain the plastic corners. We didn't know if they were for shipping or spacing. We weren't sure about the braces, which way to attach, or how far back to place the washer in the cabinet. We had to buy an extension for the drain hose. Our cabinet is right next to the sink, and it seemed that the one supplied should have been long enough. I ran my first wash, and the Control Panel was not user friendly. I read the instructions, made the actions, but was not getting the setting that I wanted. It was difficult to cancel the wash cycle that it was on to the one I preferred. I have to use the manual to remember the steps. Should be more user friendly. My first wash had dishes that had more than 24 hour dried food, which I normally would not do, but I wanted to test the dishwasher. I used Heavy Wash, and my dishes were clean! Glasses sparkled! I was very pleased. I did have some water residue on the tops of glasses. I will review the manual again for Jet Dry adjustments regarding water spots. I'm looking forward to having wash water that is softer and dishes that sparkle!

Sentence (English): I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal.
Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Sentence (English): I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal.
Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates.
