Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Sentence (English): Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people.
Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~
