Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. Before, I used to keep doing dishes while cooking, but now, even if they pile up in the sink, it's not a burden. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. It really is all so different. No matter what detergent you use, it ultimately just comes down to how much you stack or the volume of dishes. I guess that's why they say the bigger the dishwasher, the better. The dishwasher works very well! The power touch feels a bit weak, though. I often have to press it two or three times. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. But even I, who grew up eating from dishes my mom washed herself with a splatter of Pongpong and Natural Pong, am healthy, so I don't think I need to obsess over detergent too much. The only way is to buy and try different things based on experience. We all pretty much know that as long as you rinse the detergent well, that's all that matters. I poured hot water for over an hour, and soapy water only came out at the very beginning. Since mostly clear water came out in the middle and later stages, watching the water drain actually puts you at ease, so just keep an eye on it. They say if you live in a hard water area, you should just give up and install a water softener and check the water hardness, but that's such a hassle. Haha. Just wash the dishes yourself, put them in, and run the cycle with plain water without detergent. If white water stains still appear, you can rest assured knowing it's not detergent and they are just water stains. So, if you can save your wrists for a price roughly equivalent to a month's peak city gas bill in the winter, I don't see any reason to hesitate! Plus, it offers three months of interest-free installments, so there is really no burden. The drilling is just a single hole less than a centimeter deep. I have to take care of my own body, after all. I am using it with satisfaction. I see occasional reviews about breakdowns, so I'm keeping an eye on it while using it. Don't worry, let's use it together. As for cleaning the dishwasher, if you just wash the food and put it in, almost nothing accumulates. In the photo, the arrow on the circle indicates the insertion direction, and the opposite is the opening direction. You just need to twist that to remove it and wash the mesh. The tray comes out completely, making cleaning easy, and it also has a drum sterilization function. Since it is washed with hot water every day, cleaning isn't really a concern. For reference, I heard that odors and fishy water smells are issues related to cleaning and detergent. -- Additional Review --. Silicone items that are suitable for boiling water sterilization and freezing, like the ones for infants, work perfectly fine. Cooking utensils are also perfect. However, while the silicone inside the side dish lid works, you need to check if the silicone on the lid itself is synthetic, as it can bend as shown in the photo above. All stainless steel works perfectly and cleans up nicely. Coated stainless steel peeled off as shown in the photo. Coated frying pans started to lose their shine after running it three times. Generally, I do not recommend coated items because they peel off. Therefore, stainless steel, glass, ceramic, hot/cold silicone, and cooking utensil silicone are all perfectly fine. It is especially satisfying to run the silicone on side dish lids or stainless steel with stubborn grime removed. For plastic, choose #2 HDP on the bottom, or #5, which clearly says PP. You can run it without worrying about endocrine disruptors, and Tritan washes well. Since there are many types of Tritan, it works as long as it can handle both hot and cold water. I've tried Tritan food containers and tumblers, and they all worked well without deformation. I recommend all detergents: Tamsa and Bubble; you don't need to use foreign brands. I tried washing just cups for 27 minutes without quick drying, and they came out clean and residue-free. Since water quality varies, there is no reason to insist on a specific brand. Just remember to place them upside down rather than standing them upright like Tetris. If you lean them diagonally just before flipping them over, there will be no unwashed detergent residue. For the power, press and hold it rather than just tapping it briefly; it works better. Overall: It feels like someone came to my house and did the dishes for me (I love it!). Since prices keep skyrocketing, I am convinced that the sooner you buy it, the sooner you can be happy! I run it 2-3 times a day (due to vacation). When I don't run as much, I run it once in the evening. I just run it frequently without any pressure; it makes me so happy. I enjoy cooking and do it often, and I also bake. I'm the kind of mom who serves food on individual plates rather than using food containers. We are a family of four, but I don't feel like the dishwasher is too small. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Comments (English): My wrists aren't in good condition; I get inflammation in my tendons easily, and I also have tendinitis, so it hurts when I rotate them. I looked around at various options, and I thought this one wouldn't be too expensive or bulky for casual use. I paid a little over 30,000 won because of a Wow discount, but I feel like I got a really good deal. Since I read the reviews thoroughly, I expected the technician to explain things well when he came to my house, but it seems to be hit or miss. He just said, "This button is for this, this is for that, and put the detergent in here," and that was it. (I could probably figure that out just by looking at it). Anyway, he just explained the buttons like a robot and left. So, I've been watching YouTube videos and reading reviews to refer to things like how to clean it. You have to pre-soak without leaving any food residue so that there is no food getting caught in the mesh, which makes me not want to clean the dishwasher itself. So, I pre-soak the food well, roughly wipe it off with a stick scouring pad that looks like the kind used for scrubbing bathtubs, and then put it in. For a cycle of less than an hour (the time is shortened if you remove certain functions), or about an hour and 10 minutes, I could see traces of residual detergent. I ran the 1 hour and 30 minute cycle, and it came out clean without streaks. There were some water droplet marks, though. When it finishes and I hear the sound and open the door, water beads up like the frying pan in the picture. It doesn't come out completely dry. Instead, since the dishes were still warm, I opened the door, pulled out the tray, and took them out. They really dry fast. It cleans ceramics, glass, and stainless steel well, but white water droplet marks remain. At first, I thought it was detergent, but it seems like limescale. It’s exactly like how using water with limescale residue makes humidifiers and sinks whiter. You're supposed to put them in diagonally like Tetris, but it seems to work better the more you place them upside down. When placing them diagonally, it works best if you place them upside down a bit more and don't stack them vertically. That seems to be why they recommend using a wide, large dishwasher; if you're going to have a tall one, get a 2-tier model, or if it's a 1-tier model, have it wide sideways. Water jets come out in alternating streams from the top and bottom, but even though there are 4 holes, it doesn't draw water from all 4 at once. They come out in alternating pairs. Since there are small blind spots in all four corners, I packed generously into every corner. It is actually more comfortable not to try to stack things up. Dishwashers are everywhere on Carrot Market, but I specifically wanted to buy one with a stainless steel interior, so I bought a new one. I heard that the lifespan of an old dishwasher is about 5 years; back then, they were plastic, and even if it was partially stainless, I was worried about corrosion. So, I bought a new stainless steel one. It is all stainless steel except for the bottom, which is plastic. I wonder why the bottom is plastic, but well, everyone else just uses it, so I use it too. I have an old built-in 12-place setting dishwasher at home, and it is really big. The interior is plastic, and the structure is similar, but since some of it was rusty and bothered me, I ended up buying a new one. -Dishwashing Review-. As you can see in the picture, the lids got nicely warped. My resolve to just spin them because they are silicone got warped too. They say half-sized lids, plastic, coated pots, and wooden items are prohibited, but I just put a coated pot in. Something got connected and it came out. I washed it with hot water for 1 hour and 30 minutes each. It does feel a bit rough to wash, though. You can either just use stainless steel pots and skip the coating, or use it only to shorten its lifespan—it's up to you. Since using this, I use much less water and my electricity bill hasn't been high. Most importantly, I can take good care of my wrists and have more free time. Cooking feels less burdensome. It's awesome because I just soak them well, scrub them roughly with a brush, and put them in. I roughly wipe off red sauces or grease with paper towels, leftover tissues, or wet wipes. Since that's what I always do anyway, it's fine. Lastly, about the detergent. I heard that Ecover requires cutting the 6-person capacity bottles, which is inconvenient. Since it's cumbersome and I don't like the dust flying around, I bought two small detergents suitable for 6 people. With the Tamsa one, even after finishing, there is still white detergent powder left, making the cups unusable. On top of that, the grease is still there. It works well with ceramics, though. Sigh. They say it produces bubbles, but even that leaves white water droplets behind. Still, I'm somewhat satisfied with the bubble function. I feel like kicking the Tamsa in the side. But then, I put in just a few dishes and turned everything upside down to wash them. It cleaned so well! (I wondered if it was shy or playing hard to get). Well, it might depend on how you use it, so I'm still experimenting, but it's difficult. I've already repurchased the Tamsa; the 8-gram size is perfect for small loads. When there is a lot of grease, I use the bubble function and everything cleans well (I was completely mistaken all along~). They say adding rinse aid creates a coating that prevents streaks, but there are a lot of rumors that rinse aid is bad for your health. My dilemma is growing. Should I just buy EcoVer and go through the hassle of cutting it? My 고민 is getting deeper and deeper (I plan not to do that). Instead of playing Tetris, I put in a very small amount and laid it down just before turning it upside down. When I did that, both the Tamsa and the bubble function worked well. Even running it on standard mode without the drying function, it cleaned well without leaving any residue. It’s not so much about the detergent itself, but rather the way you should pour it in—not standing dishes upright in the sink, and not stacking them upside down. If you do that, there is absolutely no residue. So lately, I’ve been mainly using the smaller Tamsa brand. When the dishes are greasy and there are a lot of them, I use the larger Bubble brand. I’ve tried both Tamsa and Bubble, and they’re pretty good. As long as you manage the amount of dishes properly, and avoid overlapping or obscuring them, residue might remain, so you don’t really need to blame the detergent. I wonder why German brands like this don't have a detergent specifically for 6 people. I’ve heard that all-in-one detergents aren't good, and some people say they use a very small amount of mild regular detergent. Some people say they don't use all-in-one detergent. Others say they skip the conditioner. Still others insist you can't do it without it. And yet another person says they only use it with plain water after scrubbing with dish soap. I wonder if my hands are just too dry? -_-a. The conclusion is: it's just a matter of whether to use Type 1 or Type 2 detergent, and it's just a dilemma. Type 1 feels mild but doesn't clean as thoroughly, while people worry about residue with Type 2. The only thought I have is, "Maybe I should buy a bigger one next time?" I'm using it very, very well without any worries. Once you buy it, you'll think, "Why did I wait so long to buy this?" Let's protect our wrists, backs, and neck discs together. This is a compilation of my thoughts based on what I learned on YouTube and what I read, combined with my personal experience. I hope it helps. That's the end of my review of a product I bought with my own money~~~

Since there are no LG repair centers paid $267 out of pocket to fix. Now certified OEM replacement for the control panel assembly is malfunctioning, just like the original one. I did purchase an extended warranty on all replacement parts. Here's the kicker. the control panel assembly has been discontinued and there are NO substitute parts! Only option now is to buy a new dishwasher. Just an FYI l am meticulous about doing routine machine maintenance and upkeep and making sure dishes are thoroughly scraped before washing. This was not user error.

Sentence (English): I have had this product since July 22.
Comments (English): [ Be careful with the black model! ] || ---------------- || I have had this product since July 22. About a month ago, the black film that covers the dishwasher door began to deteriorate in one corner and every day it falls off a little more. They claim that the damage is the result of a blow - based exclusively on a photograph that I have sent them -, when it is clearly a manufacturing problem or the use of external materials of the lowest quality. The thing is that the device has not suffered any damage, but it is my word against yours (no one has come to verify that I am right).
Comments (Original): [ ¡Cuidado con el modelo color negro! ] || ---------------- || Tengo este producto desde Julio del 22. Me he puesto en contacto con  el servicio técnico de LG y me han respondido que ese desperfecto no lo cubre la garantía. Aducen que el desperfecto es producto de un golpe- basándose exclusivamente en una fotografía que les he enviado-, cuando se trata claramente de un problema de fabricación o del uso de unos materiales externos de ínfima calidad. La cuestión es que el aparato no ha sufrido ningún golpe, pero es mi palabra contra la suya (nadie ha venido a comprobar que estoy en lo cierto).

Comments (English): [ Not Impressed ] || ---------------- || I was really expecting more from this product. The inside of the washer is smaller than any of the 3 other modern dishwashers I have owned. The silverware holders will not stay attached to the bottom rack as the clip on the holders are designed to accomplish. The fold down pointy things at the back of the bottom rack will fall down at the lightest touch. The door has a spring on it that will slam it shut once it reaches about 3/4s of the way to closed, so everytime you close the door you have to manually follow it all the way to closed or the door slams against the unit. The pointy things on the bottom rack are leaning instead of being straight up. Didn't know this would be disappointing until I used it. In a modern dishwasher there really is no reason for an On/Off button, the unit should start when you press start and stop when it is finished or the door is opened. I thought Bosch was a premium brand. If it is then they really missed the mark on this model.

The side shelf to maybe hold a wine glass stem or small item makes it hard to put anything below it. Comments (English): [ I'm very satisfied even if it doesn't seat 12 people. ] || ---------------- || * Purchase Date: 23/11/03. * Satisfaction: 4.5. * I used a 12-place setting dishwasher at my previous home, but I had to move. It was difficult to install a dishwasher at the new house, so I just did the dishes by hand. It was sooooo tiring to go from using a dishwasher to washing by hand. The only option was a 6-place setting dishwasher, but no matter how I looked at it, it seemed way too small. I wondered if anything could really be done with it, so I just lived with it for 2-3 months, but I couldn't stand it anymore. I decided to buy at least this, so I searched on Coupang and purchased it. * In conclusion, I am very satisfied. The reason I decided on this model after searching for various 6-place setting dishwashers is: 1. There were quite a few 6-place setting models that didn't have an automatic door opening feature after washing. This feature is essential. Even if the inside is dried at high temperature, it feels a bit unsettling if the door doesn't open. It would be great if I could open it immediately, but since I might be out for a long time, I prioritized the automatic door opening feature. 2. I also looked at 6-place setting models that had two tiers to fit more items, but... I was tempted at first. But as I kept looking at it, the bottom space seemed too low. I felt like I wouldn't be able to fit large dishes, and it looked like it would be a bit difficult to put things in and take them out. So, I chose the 1-tier model. There is a tiny space on one side that fits the 2nd tier, though. It’s only big enough for ladles and tongs. 3. Since after-sales service is important, I chose between Samsung and LG. However, LG is expensive. The features seem similar, though. Hmm. 4. I also liked the clean, minimalist white design. ** I am leaving a review after using it for 3 months. First of all, although the space is smaller than the 12-place setting model, I liked that I could run it immediately. With the 12-place model, it wouldn't fill up all at once, so I used to combine the leftovers from dinner to run it. You can run it by only filling the top section, but the cleaning power drops when you do that. So, I was fine with the 6-place setting model because I can run it immediately. The cleaning power wasn't inferior to the 12-place model either. As long as you adjust the amount of detergent according to whether there is grease or not, the dishes always come out clean. I was especially worried that the cutlery wouldn't be cleaned properly since I run it standing upright. But the cutlery comes out sparkling clean. I was hesitant about the 6-place setting because I thought it might not be good, but I suffered for nothing for the past three months. For those of you who can't install a large dishwasher due to space constraints, don't hesitate to buy this. My wrists are precious, after all. ^^ -------------------------------------------- If my review was helpful, please press the . button. Thank you so much! ^^

It was difficult to install a dishwasher at the new house, so I just did the dishes by hand. It was sooooo tiring to go from using a dishwasher to washing by hand. The only option was a 6-place setting dishwasher, but no matter how I looked at it, it seemed way too small. I wondered if anything could really be done with it, so I just lived with it for 2-3 months, but I couldn't stand it anymore. I decided to buy at least this, so I searched on Coupang and purchased it. * In conclusion, I am very satisfied. The reason I decided on this model after searching for various 6-place setting dishwashers is: 1. There were quite a few 6-place setting models that didn't have an automatic door opening feature after washing. This feature is essential. Even if the inside is dried at high temperature, it feels a bit unsettling if the door doesn't open. It would be great if I could open it immediately, but since I might be out for a long time, I prioritized the automatic door opening feature. 2. I also looked at 6-place setting models that had two tiers to fit more items, but... I was tempted at first. But as I kept looking at it, the bottom space seemed too low. I felt like I wouldn't be able to fit large dishes, and it looked like it would be a bit difficult to put things in and take them out. So, I chose the 1-tier model. The cleaning power wasn't inferior to the 12-place model either. As long as you adjust the amount of detergent according to whether there is grease or not, the dishes always come out clean. I was especially worried that the cutlery wouldn't be cleaned properly since I run it standing upright. But the cutlery comes out sparkling clean. I was hesitant about the 6-place setting because I thought it might not be good, but I suffered for nothing for the past three months. For those of you who can't install a large dishwasher due to space constraints, don't hesitate to buy this. Sentence (English): This dishwasher does the job OK.
Comments (English): [ Does the job OK ] || ---------------- || This dishwasher does the job OK. Maybe I am just not used to prices these days, and maybe our dishes are odd sized. But for more than $1200. including our state's 10% tax for an easy installation, I expected more. First the good news. This dishwasher is super quiet. Its good they have that red right at its bottom. Otherwise, it would be hard to know if it was working. It cleans dishes as well as any dishwasher too. So no big complaints. The bad news is there's only one half sized silverware holder. We had to pay for a second one. The flat rack at the very top is a nice addition for cooking utensils and the adjustability of the other racks' heights are a help for taller items. Otherwise the interior racks don't aid efficient use of space as well as other dishwashers we've had. Finally, the drying function is energy efficient, particularly if one hits 'Air dry'. The down side is we find any little place where water can pool in a dish, it does. So at least some of our dishes usually come out with water somewhere.

Comments (English): [ Can't go wrong with Bosch! ] || ---------------- || After 15 years, our previous Bosch dishwasher finally gave out. It does an excellent job cleaning, and it dries dishes better than our old one. We've had it for about a month and I'm still experimenting with where certain dishes fit best. but that's part of the fun! Also, the upper 2 racks don't glide in & out of the dishwasher easily, so they cause all the dishes to get jerked around when you move the racks. This can cause glasses to fall over and wet dishes can pour water all over the dishes below. Other than these two issues, I'd say this dishwasher is just about perfect!

Sentence (English): I've had it for two weeks and I'm more than satisfied.
Comments (English): [ Very good quality-price ratio. ] || ---------------- || I've had it for two weeks and I'm more than satisfied. For about €350 that I was able to get it, I can't be more than happy. It has a basic 50' program but it doesn't finish drying completely and the only negative thing is that the eco program lasts approximately 3 hours (I don't see the point in this) however I haven't noticed an increase in the electricity bill compared to the previous dishwasher I had. Regarding transportation and installation, I have to say that they were two people who were in a hurry for everything. As soon as I opened the door they rushed in with everything and package to enter. They left my kitchen in a mess even though I left everything tidied up to make installation easier for them and well. Not polite treatment on the part of the installers. Garbage was left on the landing which I had to pick up since the service included unpacking but in the end I can't ask for more for the €20 cost of transport and assembly.
Comments (Original): [ Relación calidad precio muy buena. ] || ---------------- || Llevo dos semanas con el y estoy más que satisfecho. Por unos 350€ que lo pude pillar no puedo estar más que contento. Tiene un programa básico de 50’ pero no termina de secar del todo y lo único negativo es que el programa eco dura 3 horas aprox( no le veo sentido a esto) sin embargo tampoco he notado una subida en la factura de la luz respecto al anterior lavavajillas que tenía.Respecto al transporte y la instalación he de decir que eran dos personas que tenían prisa para todo. Nada más abrir la puerta se abalanzaron con todo y paquete para entrar.Me dejaron la cocina hecha un cristo a pesar de que dejé todo recogido para que les facilitara la instalación y bueno. Un trato nada educado por parte de los instaladores. Se dejaron basura por el rellano la cual tuve que recoger ya que el servicio incluía desembalaje pero al final no puedo pedir más por 20€ que cuesta el transporte y montaje.

Sentence (English): I chose this brand because of its reliability because I previously had one for 17 years and it never gave me any problems.

Dishwashers with quality finishes, with many options in terms of programs and finishes. It also has extra drying, intensive cleaning if there is a lot of dirt, for example for pots, pans, etc. and for me the best of all to gain capacity is the third cutlery tray leaving free space on the lower tray. Por lo demás perfecto.

Comments (English): [ It is not a realiable dishwasher, worked 2.5 years ] || ---------------- || We bought this (LDFN4542W) dishwasher 2.5 years ago. My wife liked how it worked, except for the touch buttons that I accidentally pressed every time I unloaded it. However, the pump died after 2.5 years. I can do a pump replacement by myself, but still, ~$340 for a part is half of its price. The support team tried to be helpful, but after 3 days of communication, I have 0 results. The Presidential Liaison Team just gave a courtesy call which I couldn't take at that moment; I responded to their SMS, and I never heard from them again. Sorry LG, but this is not what people want or expect from such a brand. I wish we could all pay a little more and have appliances and companies that care about quality. LG, you've lost another customer.

Sentence (English): As a single-person household, I debated countless times whether or not to buy a dishwasher, watching many videos on YouTube.
Comments (English): [ Great value Samsung dishwasher! ] || ---------------- || As a single-person household, I debated countless times whether or not to buy a dishwasher, watching many videos on YouTube. I really agonized over it. However, since I wasn't in a hurry, I put the idea aside for a while. But every time I did the dishes, the word "leverage" wouldn't leave my mind, so I finally decided to buy one. I'm sure everyone weighs their options before making a purchase, right? I certainly did. Price - Around 390,000 won. Initially, I considered a 3-person Minix model, but the price was similar to a 6-person dishwasher, so I hesitated a lot. On the other hand, the 3-person model in the 200,000 won range was relatively cheap, so I had doubts about whether the dishes would actually be cleaned well. Ultimately, I chose the Samsung 6-person model because of its brand reputation, capacity, and price of under 400,000 won. Features - Does it wash well? Yes, it washes well. It even has an automatic door opening feature. Since there was a significant price difference between the 3-person and 6-person models, I looked into what the difference was and found it was the direction of the water flow. Dishwashers are categorized into types that spray water from all sides, as well as those that spray from the top and bottom or only from the bottom. This product sprays water from both the top and bottom. Consequently, its cleaning power was excellent. Although it is a 6-place setting model, I was concerned about its cleaning performance given its relatively low price; however, the conclusion is that cleaning performance is not an issue! It even features an automatic door opening function, so you don't have to worry about water condensation even if you run the dishwasher and go out. Design - Simple, modern white BESPOKE. Thanks to the sophisticated white Bespoke design that looks stylish and fits well anywhere, my dull kitchen has brightened up. It's a real charm that grows on you! Brand - Samsung. I watched several YouTube videos, and it turned out that most small dishwasher manufacturers were Chinese brands. Cuckoo, SK Magic, Samsung, etc., were all from the same manufacturer. This product is no exception, but since it bears the Samsung brand, it instantly elevates the quality, so I tend to forget about the manufacturer. I spend 20 to 30 minutes washing dishes, and sometimes I get a reality check. I keep thinking "leverage, leverage," but my wallet is light, so I hesitated. I rationalized it by telling myself that it was worth buying if it was under 400,000 won. If I have a dishwasher, I can read at least one more page, get a little more exercise, and save more water and gas! Please rationalize it. ------------. Cons. I received it on December 19th and have been using it for over a month, and I swear I haven't found a single flaw. It is the most satisfying product I have ever bought. Price - Around 390,000 won. Initially, I considered a 3-person Minix model, but the price was similar to a 6-person dishwasher, so I hesitated a lot. It even has an automatic door opening feature. Since there was a significant price difference between the 3-person and 6-person models, I looked into what the difference was and found it was the direction of the water flow. Dishwashers are categorized into types that spray water from all sides, as well as those that spray from the top and bottom or only from the bottom. That one dries very good and I didn't mind may a couple of hundred more to know my dishes will be dry when I take them out. The other thing I didn't like about this unit for that the countdown timer was on top of the unit. You cant really see it when the door is closed. The upgraded model has the number displayed on the front of the unit you can see it from across the room no problem.
